note: Authored Study Room quiz items. Code items are validated by execution. Module items (generics, collections-contracts, streams, concurrency): snippets, compile-error claims and outputs executed on the JDK; wildcard/PECS signatures compile-checked. JUnit items are not executed (JUnit is not installed) and are grounded in the knowledge base only.

items.prompt: Integer is a subtype of Number. Why does `List<Number> nums = new ArrayList<Integer>();` not compile?
choices: ArrayList<Integer> is a raw type, and raw types cannot be assigned to a parameterized variable
Number is abstract, so it cannot be used as a type argument of List
Generics are invariant: allowing it would let a Double be added to a list of Integers
Type erasure removes Integer, so the compiler cannot tell the two lists apart
items.explanation: List<Integer> is not a subtype of List<Number>. If it were, code could insert a Double through the List<Number> reference into a list that must hold only Integers.

items.prompt: A generic method must copy every element of a source list into a destination list: `static <T> void copyAll(?? src, ?? dst)`. Which parameter types follow the producer-extends, consumer-super guideline?
choices: List<? super T> src, List<? extends T> dst
List<? extends T> src, List<? extends T> dst
List<? extends T> src, List<? super T> dst
items.explanation: The source only produces values, so it is `? extends T`; the destination only consumes values, so it is `? super T`. A `List<?>` or `? extends T` destination cannot accept additions.

items.prompt: Inside `class Box<T> { ... }`, which of these statements does not compile?
items.explanation: Generic arrays cannot be created because T is erased at run time and the array's element type could not be checked. Pass an IntFunction<T[]> or use a List<T> instead.

items.prompt: sumAll(int[] values) should return the sum of the values, but the class does not compile. Repair the helper's parameter type so any list of numbers can be passed in.
items.explanation: The helper only reads from the list, so it should accept `List<? extends Number>`; List<Integer> is not a List<Number>.

items.prompt: In your own words: why does the compiler reject `numbers.add(Integer.valueOf(1))` when `numbers` is declared as `List<? extends Number>`?
items.answer: The wildcard means the list's real element type is some unknown subtype of Number. The reference might point at a List<Double>, so the compiler cannot prove an Integer is safe to insert. Only null can be added, while reads are fine and give Number.

items.prompt: Which of these PriorityQueue operations does the documentation list as linear time?
items.explanation: PriorityQueue is a heap: offer and poll are O(log n), peek is O(1), but contains (like remove(Object)) must scan the elements.

items.prompt: Your test prints the elements of a HashSet<String> and passes today. What does the API documentation say about relying on that order?
choices: It is insertion order as long as nothing has been removed
It is sorted by each element's hash code, so it is predictable
It stays the same for a given set of elements on every JVM run
It makes no guarantee, and the order can change over time
items.explanation: HashSet and HashMap promise no iteration order. Use LinkedHashSet for insertion order or TreeSet for sorted order.

items.prompt: isLess(int a, int b) should report whether a sorts before b, the test a comparator would make. It gives wrong answers for some extreme values. Fix it.
items.explanation: a - b can overflow for large or negative ints. Integer.compare never subtracts.

items.prompt: A TreeSet<Employee> built with a comparator on salary silently lost an employee whose name differs from everyone else's. In your own words, explain why it was lost and what to change.
items.answer: A TreeSet decides whether two elements are duplicates using only the comparator, never equals. Two employees whose salaries compare as 0 are treated as the same element, so the second add is ignored. Add a tie-breaker such as thenComparing on a unique field so the ordering is consistent with equals.

items.prompt: Which statement about parallel streams is consistent with the Stream documentation?
choices: A parallel stream is faster than a sequential one once the source holds a few thousand elements
Calling parallel() makes a lambda that appends to a shared ArrayList thread-safe
A parallel stream is not automatically faster, and it does not make shared mutable state safe
Lambdas in a parallel pipeline always run in the source's encounter order
items.explanation: Speed depends on source size, splitting, operation cost and the environment, so measure. Shared mutation stays unsafe; prefer a collector or reduction.

items.prompt: sumPositive(int[] a) should return the sum of the positive values, but the class does not compile. Repair it using a reduction rather than mutating a captured variable.
items.explanation: A lambda can only capture effectively final locals. A terminal reduction such as sum() avoids the external accumulator, and is also safe in parallel.

items.prompt: Write countLong(String[] words, int minLen) that returns how many words have at least minLen characters. Use a stream pipeline.
items.explanation: filter keeps matching words and count() is the terminal operation; count returns long, so cast it to int.

items.prompt: A teammate claims that the line `names.stream().map(String::trim);` has already trimmed every name. In your own words, what is wrong with that claim?
items.answer: Intermediate operations such as map are lazy: calling them only describes the pipeline. Nothing is traversed until a terminal operation such as collect, count or reduce runs, and the result of that line is just an unconsumed stream. The source list is never modified.

items.prompt: A task catches InterruptedException from a blocking call and cannot rethrow it. What should it normally do?
choices: Log it and carry on, because catching the exception already ended the interruption request
Call Thread.currentThread().stop() so the thread cannot keep running
Restore the flag with Thread.currentThread().interrupt() and stop the interrupted work
Ignore it, since interruption only applies to virtual threads
items.explanation: Interruption is a cooperative signal. Throwing InterruptedException clears the flag, so code that cannot propagate it should restore the flag and stop what it was doing.

items.prompt: `cf.cancel(true)` is called on a CompletableFuture while its supplier is still running. According to the documentation, what happens?
choices: The thread running the supplier is interrupted and the supplier stops early
It completes with CancellationException, but the computation keeps running
The call blocks until the supplier finishes, then completes the future normally
Nothing happens, because a future whose work has started cannot be cancelled
items.explanation: cancel(true) completes the future with CancellationException, but the documentation says it does not interrupt the computation, so long-running suppliers need their own cancellation check.

items.prompt: A service moves to virtual threads, but its database allows only 20 concurrent connections. How should that limit be enforced?
choices: Bound access to the database, for example with a semaphore around the calls
Create a pool of 20 virtual threads, because virtual threads are expensive to create
Do nothing: virtual threads remove database and memory limits
Switch back to platform threads, which throttle database calls automatically
items.explanation: Virtual threads are cheap, so you should not pool them to limit concurrency. They do not lift downstream limits; admission to the scarce resource must be bounded explicitly.

items.prompt: doubledSum(int a, int b) should return (a + b) * 2 using chained futures, but the class does not compile. Fix the chain.
items.explanation: thenApply wraps the returned future, giving CompletableFuture<CompletableFuture<Integer>>. thenCompose flattens it.

items.prompt: In your own words: when the next step of a CompletableFuture chain itself returns a CompletableFuture, why use thenCompose rather than thenApply?
items.answer: thenApply wraps whatever the function returns, so a function that returns a future produces a nested CompletableFuture<CompletableFuture<T>> that still has to be unwrapped. thenCompose flattens it, like flatMap, so the chain continues with the inner future's result.

items.prompt: With default JUnit Jupiter settings, which rule applies to a @BeforeAll method?
choices: It must be an instance method, because it runs before each test instance exists
It must be static, unless the class uses @TestInstance(Lifecycle.PER_CLASS)
It must also carry @Test, or the runner ignores it
It must be public, and the test class must be public too
items.explanation: @BeforeAll and @AfterAll run once per class, so by default they are static. PER_CLASS lifecycle lets them be instance methods. Jupiter test classes and methods need not be public.

items.prompt: With default Jupiter settings, what happens when both tests run, in either order?
choices: Whichever test runs second fails, because calls is already 1
Neither compiles, because test instance fields must be static
Both fail, because calls starts at 0 and the assertion expects 1
Both pass: each test method gets its own new instance of the class
items.explanation: Jupiter creates a new test-class instance for every test method, so the field starts at 0 each time and instance state does not leak between tests.

items.prompt: A build passes but reports 0 tests. The test class imports @Test from org.junit.Test (JUnit 4), and the build only has the Jupiter engine. Why are no tests found?
choices: Jupiter tests must be public methods declared in public classes
Jupiter does not discover methods annotated with the JUnit 4 @Test
@Test only takes effect when the class also declares a @BeforeAll method
assertEquals was not statically imported, so the whole class was skipped
items.explanation: Jupiter's annotations live in org.junit.jupiter.api. Mixing in JUnit 4's @Test is a common reason tests silently do not run.

items.prompt: What does `assertThrows(IllegalArgumentException.class, () -> graph.addEdge(-1, 0))` return when the exception is thrown?
choices: Nothing, so the exception message cannot be inspected
true, meaning the expected exception type was thrown
The value that addEdge would have returned
The thrown exception, so its message can be checked
items.explanation: assertThrows returns the exception it caught, so a test can assert on getMessage() as well as the type.

items.prompt: A test file using @ParameterizedTest fails to compile because org.junit.jupiter.params cannot be found, though @Test from Jupiter works. Which dependency is missing?
choices: junit-jupiter-params, included in the junit-jupiter aggregate
junit-vintage-engine, the engine that runs parameterized tests
mockito-core, the library that supplies parameter sources
items.explanation: Parameterized tests need the junit-jupiter-params artifact. Vintage runs old JUnit 3/4 tests, and Mockito and AssertJ are separate libraries.

items.prompt: A unit test passes when run by itself but fails when the whole build runs. In your own words, what kind of hidden coupling could cause this, and how would you make the test reliable?
items.answer: Tests can depend on shared static state, a clock, an external service, or on running after another test. Leftover state from an earlier test changes the result, so the outcome depends on execution order. Make each test set up its own fresh state, for example in @BeforeEach, clean up what it owns, and never depend on another test running first.

items.prompt: In your own words: what does JUnit Jupiter do by default so that fields set in one test method are not visible in the next one?
items.answer: By default Jupiter creates a new instance of the test class for each test method, so every test starts with fresh field values and nothing is shared. @BeforeEach runs around every test for per-test setup, while @BeforeAll runs once and has to be static unless the class opts into the PER_CLASS lifecycle.
